This is a claim petition under Section 166 and 140 of M.V. Act regarding injury sustained by petitioner Chander Kant Tiwari in a roadside accident occurred on 24.09.2015.

As per the averments in the claim petition, it is stated that on 24.09.2015 at about 8.15 p.m. when he was returning from his relatives home to his home and reached near C.M. Hospital, 100 Foota Road while on a bicycle, suddenly a motor biker hit the petitioner from his back.

It is stated that registration number of offending vehicle/motor bike was PB-13V-2010 which was being driven by MACT No.1060/2016 by SHAILENDER Page 1 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.04.12 16:28:03 +0530 respondent no.1 in a high speed and in a rash and negligent manner.
It is stated that due to such impact, petitioner fell down on the road and received multiple injuries including fractures.
Petitioner was taken to C.M. Hospital where doctors referred him to GTB Hospital.
On the statement of the injured, FIR No.806/2015, PS Jyoti Nagar under Section 279/337 IPC was registered on 02.10.2015.
It is stated that the accident has occurred due to rash and negligent driving of respondent no.1.
It is stated that respondent no.2 is the registered owner of the offending vehicle and it was not insured.
2. It is stated that petitioner at the time of accident was working in Globe Sanitation factory at Jhilmil Industrial Area as a worker of brass water tab and was earning Rs.12,000/- per month.

Issue No.1 7.
It is settled proposition of law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.

Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition Chander Kant Tiwari vs Daljeet Singh on 12 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/45522650/

Issue No.2 12.
The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd. 1995 AIR 755.

entities.text: R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd. 1995 AIR 755
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant extract is as under:
"Broadly speaking while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which is capable of being calculated in terms of money-, whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may, include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit upto the date of trial; (iii) other material loss.
So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned

,
they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit;
(iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e. on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, MACT No.1060/2016 SHAILENDER Page 6 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date:
2024.04.12 16:28:46 +0530 discomfort, disappointment, hardship, frustration and mental stress in life."
13. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.

sentences.text: The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

5. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary Damages (special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment.
 (b) Loss of future earnings on account of MACT No.1060/2016 by SHAILENDER Page 7  SHAILENDER MALIK  MALIK Date: 2024.04.12  16:28:56 +0530  permanent disability.
 (iii) Future medical expenses.
 Non-Pecuniary Damages (general damages)
 (iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a  consequence of the injuries.
 (v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects  of marriage)
 (vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of  normal longevity).

In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i),
(ii), (a) and (iv).

It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii), (b), (iii), (v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
14.

In the light of the aforementioned judgments, the compensation to which the petitioner is entitled shall be as under:-
PECUNIARY DAMAGES :
Medical Expenses:
15.

Petitioner/inured (PW1) in his deposition stated that after the accident he was taken to C.M.
Hospital where doctors referred him to GTB Hospital, Delhi.
It is claimed by the petitioner that he incurred expenses of Rs.23,000/- on his medical treatment.
Petitioner has proved medical prescription as Ex.PW1/2 and medical bills as Ex.PW1/3.
Perusal of original medical invoices/bills Ex.PW1/3 placed on judicial record shows that a total sum of Rs.23,358/- was spent by the petitioner on his medicines, surgical items, etc.
There is nothing contrary on the record to the medical bills/invoices proved by the petitioner.

As such this Tribunal awards a MACT No.1060/2016 by SHAILENDER Page 8 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.04.12 16:29:04 +0530 compensation of Rs.23,358/- to the petitioner under the head of medical expenses.

Loss of earning during treatment:
16.

As per petitioner (PW1) he was working in Globe Sanitation factory no.10 at Jhilmil Industrial Area (near Hero Honda) Delhi as a worker of brass water tab and at the time of accident his salary was Rs.12,000/- per month and after doing over time work it will come around Rs.14,000/- to Rs.15,000/- per month.

To prove the work and income as claimed, petitioner has examined PW2 Sunil Diwakar, proprietor of firm by name and style M/s Globe Enterprises who deposed that his firm is dealing with the business of manufacturing of brass tabs.
PW2 deposed that petitioner Chander Kant Tiwari was working as fitter in his firm since incorporation in the year 2010 and was drawing a salary of Rs.14,000/- per month.
Witness says that petitioner is not reporting to his job since September 2015.
17. So far as testimony of PW2 is concerned, he has not brought any document in support of his testimony that he is running any firm M/s Globe Enterprises.
Said witness has not produced any document to show that any such firm was registered.
He has also not produced any attendance record of his employees or appointment letter of petitioner to show that petitioner was working in his said firm as fitter.
PW2 has also not produced any salary slip of the petitioner to show that he was drawing salary of Rs.14,000/- per month.
In the absence of any such document, testimony of PW2 is only oral one and there is no basis to substantiate his version.

Even otherwise PW1/petitioner admitted in his cross examination that he has not filed any record of his Chander Kant Tiwari vs Daljeet Singh on 12 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/45522650/

19. Petitioner/injured in his evidence has proved documents Ex.PW1/2 and MLC regarding nature of injuries, medical treatment record etc.

From the perusal of those documents it is evident that petitioner beside suffering accidental injuries i.e. fracture on his left leg, had medical complications due to those accidental injuries and had to undergo bone grafting by way of surgery conducted in GTB hospital.

Petitioner has also examined PW3 Dr.Himanshu from GTB Hospital who proved disability certificate of the petitioner Ex.PW3/A whereby medical board assessed the permanent disability of the petitioner to the extent of 13% in relation to left lower limb.
Unfortunately whatever medical documents have been proved on the record, there is no specific evidence as for which period petitioner remained hospitalized and took the treatment.
However the Tribunal being duty bound to award just and fair compensation, has to take the evidence as come on the record to decide the question by preponderance of probability.

Accordingly petitioner is granted compensation for loss of income during treatment i.e. Rs.54,288/- (Rs.9,048 X 06 months).

Loss of future earning due to disability :
20.

In case of Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India determined the broad criteria for assessment of permanent disability for ascertaining the purpose of future loss of earning and also laid down step by step procedure for assessment of disability and for ascertainment to the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity.

sentences.text:
Relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:-
"9.
Therefore, the Tribunal has to first decide whether there is any permanent disability and if so, the extent of such permanent disability.

This means that the tribunal should consider and decide with reference to the evidence:
(i) Whether the disablement is permanent or temporary;

sentences.text: (ii) If the disablement is permanent, whether it is permanent total disablement or permanent partial disablement;

(iii) If the disablement percentage is expressed with reference to any specific limb,
then the effect of such disablement of the limb on the functioning of the entire body,
that is the permanent disability suffered by the person.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
But if the Tribunal concludes that there is permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.

After the Tribunal ascertains the actual MACT No.1060/2016 by SHAILENDER Page 11 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.04.12 16:29:30 +0530 extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.
10. Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) Whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood."
....If doctor has given evidence about percentage of permanent disability, Tribunal will have to seek doctors opinion as to whether it is possible to deduce the corresponding functional permanent disability with reference to whole body and if so to what percentage.

13. We may now summarize the principles discussed above:
(i). All injuries (or permanent disabilities arising from injuries), do not result in loss of earning capacity.
(ii). The percentage of permanent disability with reference to the whole body of a person, cannot be assumed to be the percentage of loss of earning capacity.

To put it differently, the percentage of loss of earning capacity is not the same as the percentage of MACT No.1060/2016 by SHAILENDER Page 12 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.04.12 16:29:38 +0530 permanent disability (except in a few cases, where the Tribunal on the basis of evidence, concludes that percentage of loss of earning capacity is the same as percentage of permanent disability).

21.

Hon'ble Apex Court in the matter of Raj Kumar vs. Ajay Kumar (supra) has laid down that Tribunal is bound to assess the evidence on the record, for the purpose of ascertaining the functional disability of the petitioner on account of medical permanent disability to assess how much the medical disability adversely affected on the functional capacity of the petitioner/injured so that just and fair amount of compensation can be ascertained under the heading of future loss of earning.

22. Keeping in view the ratio as discussed above, in the evidence of PW1 he has given all the details of treatment taken by him at GTB Hospital vide OPD/medical treatment documents vide Ex.PW1/2 as well as about the nature of injuries suffered by him.
Beside this it has also come on the record that petitioner suffered permanent disability to the extent of 13%, permanent disability certificate is Ex.PW1/6 (Ex.PW3/A) in relation to left lower limb.

The nature of the job of the petitioner has already been discussed above as petitioner was working as fitter and doing work of brass MACT No.1060/2016 by SHAILENDER Page 13 SHAILENDER MALIK MALIK Date: 2024.04.12 16:30:16 +0530
water tab
, due to the accidental injuries evidently petitioner could not work efficiently as he suffered the injury in relation to left lower limb.
As such given the nature of the job, nature of injuries and permanent disability suffered by the petitioner, this Tribunal finds that petitioner had 13% functional disability.
23. Further, law is well settled that there should be no departure from the multiplier method in injury cases also [refer: Sandeep Khanuja vs. Atul Dande & Anr., (2017) 3 SCC 351].

As such at the time of accident on 24.09.2015 petitioner was around 47 years of age.

As such multiplier to be applied in the present case would be 13 as applicable to age group between 46 to 50 years, would be applicable as per settled principle laid down in case of Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121.

Moreover, the law has been well settled by the decisions of Supreme Court in the cases of Sandeep Khanuja (supra) and Erudhaya Priya vs. State Express Transport Corporation Ltd., 2020 SCC OnLine SC 601, that while applying the multiplier method, future prospects on advancement in life and career are also to be taken into consideration.

Special Diet & Conveyance Charges:
25.
In the written submissions filed on behalf of petitioner, a sum of Rs.2,50,000/- under the head of pain and suffering, special diet, conveyance charges etc. have been claimed.

Though it is matter of record that petitioner has proved in his evidence his medical treatment documents, but no documentary evidence in the form of prescription of doctor or bills of transportation and special diet has been placed on record to substantiate his claim that he has incurred any expenses towards conveyance and special diet.

In the absence of any such documentary proof, this Tribunal while taking into consideration period of medical treatment of petitioner, nature of injuries and the extent of permanent disability suffered by him, finds it appropriate to grant compensation for a sum of Rs.20,000/- towards conveyance charges and a sum of Rs.20,000/- towards special diet.

Attendant Charges:
26.

Petitioner in his affidavit deposed that he is still bed ridden as per doctors advise and he is unable to do his basic daily routine without the assistance of an attendant for which petitioner is stated to be paying Rs.5,000/- per month to such an attendant for last 18 months.
However fact remains that no evidence has been placed on record to substantiate such claim.
Even no documentary evidence has been placed on record in support of same.
Nor any witness has been examined by the petitioner to the effect that services of any attendant were engaged by him.

However this Tribunal while assessing loss of income of petitioner due to accidental injuries,
assessed loss of such income for six months.
Therefore it would be in the interest of justice to grant attendant charges i.e. Rs.30,000/- (Rs.5,000/- X 06 months).

The tribunal has to first ascertain what activities of the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of permanent disability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) Whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood."

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is settled proposition of law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
As such there is sufficient material on record to establish that accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of respondent no.1 while driving offending vehicle/motorcycle no.PB-13V- 2010.
The scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/s Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd. 1995 AIR 755.
13. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.
The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.
This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii), (b), (iii), (v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
14.
Moreover evidence of that witness is without any documentary proof regarding evidence.
In the absence of same evidence of PW2 is hardly of any substance for concluding regarding exact income of the petitioner.
In such circumstances when there is no oral or documentary evidence at all on the record regarding exact income of the petitioner, this Tribunal has taken notional income of the petitioner at parity with minimum wages of an unskilled worker as applicable in Delhi at the time of accident should be invoked i.e. Rs.9,048/- per month.
However the Tribunal being duty bound to award just and fair compensation, has to take the evidence as come on the record to decide the question by preponderance of probability.
, due to the accidental injuries evidently petitioner could not work efficiently as he suffered the injury in relation to left lower limb.
As such given the nature of the job, nature of injuries and permanent disability suffered by the petitioner, this Tribunal finds that petitioner had 13% functional disability.
23. Further, law is well settled that there should be no departure from the multiplier method in injury cases also [refer: Sandeep Khanuja vs. Atul Dande & Anr., (2017) 3 SCC 351].
As such at the time of accident on 24.09.2015 petitioner was around 47 years of age.
As such multiplier to be applied in the present case would be 13 as applicable to age group between 46 to 50 years, would be applicable as per settled principle laid down in case of Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121.
Moreover, the law has been well settled by the decisions of Supreme Court in the cases of Sandeep Khanuja (supra) and Erudhaya Priya vs. State Express Transport Corporation Ltd., 2020 SCC OnLine SC 601, that while applying the multiplier method, future prospects on advancement in life and career are also to be taken into consideration.
Thus,
considering the petitioner in the age bracket of 40 to 50 years at the time of accident and was self employed, in view of the judgment in Pranay Sethi & Others (supra) an addition of income to the extent of 25% towards future prospects has to be counted.
Therefore it would be in the interest of justice to grant attendant charges i.e. Rs.30,000/- (Rs.5,000/- X 06 months).
In this case, as per medical documents of the petitioner, he was found to have suffered injuries in his left leg.
Thus, it is clear that petitioner must have suffered pain and suffering during his treatment and therefore, this Tribunal is of the opinion that an amount of Rs.50,000/- would be just and fair compensation for pain, sufferings and mental trauma suffered by the petitioner as consequences of injuries sustained in the accident.
Therefore taking into consideration nature of injuries, disability, he is awarded a sum of Rs.25,000/- under the head of loss of amenities.
This Tribunal is very much open and conscious of awarding compensation, however there must be some evidence regarding disfigurement which is different than permanent disability.
It must be borne in mind that disfigurement is different than permanent disability.
This Tribunal has already assessed compensation for future loss of income on account of permanent disability by the petitioner.
Disfigurement is in the form of disformation of limb of the petitioner.
Even if there is evidence regarding accidental injuries suffered by the petitioner, no evidence is on the record proving disformation of the body or any part of the body of the petitioner.
In such circumstance when compensation has already been awarded to the petitioner under different legally recognized heads as per the evidence available on record, no case is made out for awarding any compensation under the above head.
Since it has already been held by this Tribunal that deceased died due to rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle no.PB-13V-2010 being driven by respondent no.1 and owned by respondent no.2, therefore the amount of compensation is payable by respondent no.1 and 2 being jointly and severally liable.
